## Trainer

Choose **the band** or **a melody line**, a **tonality**, a **level**, and press **Start**. You hear three versions, A, B and C. Two of them are the same
chord progression played two different ways; the third is a slightly different progression in a third way. Pick the different one.
**Space** plays all three again, **A** / **B** / **C** answer, **N** shows or hides notation, **Enter** goes on.

Notation can be shown at any time (before you answer the chord symbols stay hidden unless you set **Notation → Chord symbols** to Always).

<div id="prog-ear"></div>

**Busyness** (under **The band**) calms the band down when a style gets too busy to hear the chords through: **Less busy** drops the
drum fills, has the bass play a two-feel (swing styles) or roots on beats 1 and 3, and the chords played steadily on the beat;
**Calm** holds each bass note and chord for its whole length over light brushes.

## The levels: the band

Each version is played by the Backing Track band in its own style (piano ballad, rock, acoustic strum, Motown, bossa nova, swing...),
with or without drums. The two same versions differ in style, and at higher levels in voicing too.

| Level | Counts as the same | What the different one changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Triads: another function | style | one chord to a chord with another job (IV for V) |
| 2 · Triads: a third away | style | one chord to a chord sharing two notes (vi for I, ii for IV) |
| 3 · Inversions are the same | inversions (3rd or 5th in the bass) | a third away, or another function |
| 4 · Sevenths are the same | sevenths added or left out | a third away |
| 5 · Reharmonised (borrowed chords off) | sevenths, inversions | another chord of the key that still holds the melody's notes |
| 5 · Borrowed and applied chords (on) | sevenths, inversions | IV to iv, ii to II7 (V/V), vi to VI7, V to bVII |
| 6 · Extensions are the same | 6, 9, 11, 13, 6/9, sus4 (two chords a bar) | a third away, or borrowed/applied |
| 7 · Reharmonised, in colour (off) | all the colours, jazz and Latin styles | a diatonic reharmonisation, or a chord a third away |
| 7 · Jazz colour: substitutes (on) | all the colours, jazz and Latin styles | bII7 for V (tritone substitute), a passing #iv°7, bVI for vi |
| 8 · Anything | everything | anything |

## Borrowed chords and reharmonising

**Borrowed chords** is off unless you turn it on. Off, every chord stays in the key (the tonality), and the "slightly different"
progression at levels 5 and 7 is a **reharmonisation**: another chord of the key that still holds the melody's notes there. A melody
resting on *so* that usually gets V could instead get I or iii (both hold *so*) and still fit. It could get IV, with *so* as IV's 9th:
the chord is played as IV(add9) for a gospel sound. On, those levels bring in borrowed, applied and chromatic chords instead.

With **A tune on top**, the band plays the same tune in all three clips. The difference is then only under the tune: listen for the
chord changing while the melody stays the same. Without it, the reharmonised chord still shares the 3rd or 5th of the chord it
replaces: the note a melody would hold there.

## Tonalities

Every level works in each of the eight tonalities in *Learning Sequences in Music* (Gordon, p. 149): major, harmonic minor, Dorian,
Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian, or **Any tonality** for a mix. Each has its own progressions, built on the chords
that make it sound like itself:

| Tonality | Typical progressions | "Cousin" change at levels 5+ (borrowed chords on) |
|---|---|---|
| Major | I–vi–IV–V, I–IV–V–I, ii–V–I | IV→iv, ii→II7, V→bVII |
| Harmonic minor | i–iv–V–i, i–bVI–bIII–bVII, i–ii°–V–i | iv→IV, V→v, ii°→ii; bII (Neapolitan) as a chromatic change |
| Dorian | i–IV–i–IV, i–bVII–IV–i | IV→iv (now Aeolian), v→V |
| Phrygian | i–bII–i–bII, i–bvii–bVI–bII | bII→ii°, bvii→bVII |
| Lydian | I–II–I–II, I–II–vii–I | II→IV or ii (now major) |
| Mixolydian | I–bVII–IV–I, I–v–IV–I | bVII→V, v→V (now major) |
| Aeolian | i–bVI–bIII–bVII, i–iv–v–i | v→V (now harmonic minor), iv→IV |
| Locrian | i°–bII–i°–bII, i°–bV–bII–i° | i°→i, bV→v |

Harmonic minor progressions also use the natural 7th's chords (bIII, bVII), as minor-key music does. In a tonality other than major, a
level whose own kind of change has no chord to work on falls back to a chord a third away or one with another function. The progressions
are this site's inventions in each tonality's idiom; the "typical" column is not taken from a source.

## The levels: a melody line

One line with no accompaniment, each version on its own instrument. The two same versions are different melodies over the same chords.

| Level | The line |
|---|---|
| 1 · Chord tones only | one chord tone a beat, the root or third on each downbeat |
| 2 · Passing tones | a passing tone may fill a third on a weak beat |
| 3 · Neighbour tones | eighth notes, passing and neighbour tones, sevenths in the line |
| 4 · Appoggiaturas and suspensions | non-chord tones on strong beats that resolve by step; two chords a bar |
| 5 · Anything | anticipations, escape tones, chromatic neighbours, chromatic chords |

After you answer, the melody notation labels each non-chord tone (P, N, CN, A, S, Ant, E).

## For teachers

- The progressions are common patterns in each tonality, written as Roman numerals and played in a random key; the voicings, styles and melodies
  are made fresh each time. They are this site's inventions, not transcriptions.
- At levels 1–3 the band's styles are pop, rock and folk; jazz styles voice chords with extensions of their own, so they come in at level 4
  (**The band → Styles** overrides this).
- Your last ten answers at each level stay in this browser; eight of ten suggests moving on.
- Related: [Hearing Harmony](harmony-ear.qmd) (naming progressions), [Bass Lines by Ear](bass-ear.qmd).
